Optimal Toolpath Design of Additive Manufactured Composite Cylindrical Structures Felipe Fernandez1, James P. Lewicki1, and Daniel A. Tortorelli1,2 1Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, California, USA 2Department of Mechanical Sciences and Engineering, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Illinois, USA January 15, 2021 Abstract Structural design optimization for additive manufacturing is primarily focused on planar layer-by- layerprocessesanddesignofcompositecylindricalstructuresdoesnotoften accommodatemanufacturing constraints. In this study, we propose to optimize the toolpath trajectory of additively manufactured compositecylinderscomprisedofmultiplethincylindricalannuli. Ourprintingprocessisbasedondirect ink writing in which short carbon fibers in a thermoset resin are extruded through a moving nozzle to build up a structure. Since the fibers are primarily aligned in the flow direction of the extrudate, the printing trajectory influences the material properties of the composite structure. To accommodate this, we define the toolpaths as contours of parameterized level-set functions. This parameterization allows us to optimize the material properties and impose manufacturing constraints such as no-overlap, no-sag, minimum radius of curvature, and continuity of the toolpaths. Several examples illustrate the optimization procedure. 1 Introduction Additive manufacturing is radically changing the design and production of a variety of products, from prosthetic limbs to components in the automotive and aerospace industries. Manufacturers are using this technology for expanding the design space, prototyping new parts, and reducing costs for production pro- cesses. In general, additive manufacturing builds solid parts by fusing material in a layer-by-layer process. This is contrary to subtractive manufacturing, which starts from a solid piece feedstock and removes mate- rial until the desired shape is achieved. In this way, additive manufacturing has a great potential to build complex shapes, reduce waste, and be more cost-effective than its subtractive counterparts. However, one of the most important advantages of additive manufacturing technology is its ability to deposit material in precise microstructures. In essence, we now have the ability to optimally place materials at the micro level so as to tailor their effective material properties at the meso and macro scale levels.
